nodes.label: Q23: Logging and monitoring in microservices
Logs, traces and metrics
nodes.rationale: Three tools answering three questions: what happened in this request, where the time went and which hop failed, and is this normal. You alert on metrics, because alerting on log lines drowns you. Debug order: metrics → traces → logs; going straight to logs is how you spend an hour reading the wrong service.

nodes.label: Correlation id propagation
nodes.rationale: Adopted not always generated, so a chain does not break at the gateway; pushed into Serilog's LogContext so every line carries it; returned on the response so a user can quote it; and written back onto the request headers so a reverse proxy forwards it — skipping that last step was a real bug. The broker hop is the one people forget, because a consumer runs on a thread with no HttpContext.

nodes.label: Structured logging
nodes.rationale: Message templates keep ProjectCode as a queryable field; string interpolation produces text you can only grep, and at nine services greppable text is not enough.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry over a vendor SDK
nodes.rationale: Instrumentation should not change when the backend does — Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb or App Insights by changing an endpoint. MassTransit's activity source is included so a trace follows a request through the broker. Health probes are filtered out because they fire constantly and bury the requests that matter.

nodes.label: What to alert on
nodes.rationale: The four golden signals plus three microservices-specific ones people forget: queue depth and dead-letter count, outbox rows unprocessed and ageing (the earliest signal that publishing has stalled), and saga instances stuck in a non-terminal state. Alert on error rate, not an individual error.

nodes.label: Correlation id vs trace id
nodes.rationale: Both, and different: W3C traceparent serves tracing tools, while the correlation id is human-friendly, survives places trace context is not propagated, and can be read off a screen and quoted to support.
